deed: Eliezer Zamenhof created Esperanto so that different peoples would understand one another
title: The Jewish ophthalmologist from Białystok who invented Esperanto, a common second language for all peoples

trailer.text: L. L. Zamenhof was a Jewish ophthalmologist from Białystok, and he is the inventor of Esperanto.
Poles, Germans, Russians and Yiddish-speaking Jews lived in his city. Each group spoke a different language, and they viewed one another with suspicion.
He believed that the main reason for the hatred and prejudice was misunderstanding, caused by the lack of one common language.
In 1887 he published the first pamphlet of the new language under the pen name Doktoro Esperanto,

glance.label: Inventor
glance.value: L. L. Zamenhof, a Jewish ophthalmologist from Białystok

glance.label: Where
glance.value: Born in Białystok, lived and worked in Warsaw

glance.label: Reached
glance.value: Asia, America, the Middle East and Africa

paragraphs.text: Zamenhof was born on 15 December 1859 in Białystok, in the Russian Empire.
He grew up in a multilingual family of educated Jews.
According to a Ministry of Education booklet, he was the eldest of nine children.
His father and his paternal grandfather were language teachers.
Poles, Germans, Russians and Yiddish-speaking Jews lived in Białystok at the end of the 19th century.
Each group spoke a different language, and they viewed members of the other communities with suspicion.
According to The Jewish Encyclopedia, four languages were spoken in the city, and to this Zamenhof attributed the dissensions and misunderstandings that disturbed it.
The quarrels between the groups saddened and frustrated him.
His parents intended him to study medicine, but his dream was to invent an international language.
He studied medicine in Moscow and Warsaw, and for years he dreamed of a way for different groups to communicate easily and peacefully.
By 1878 his language project, Lingwe uniwersala, was almost finished.
For three years Zamenhof worked on Yiddish and compiled a grammar of it.
According to another source, in 1879 he wrote one of the first grammars of Yiddish.
After the pogroms in Russia in 1882 he joined the early Zionist movement, Hibbat Zion.
He was an active member of Chovevei Zion in Warsaw and a member of its executive committee.
At an early stage he also proposed a Jewish colony in the Mississippi River valley.
Within a few years he lost faith in Zionism and turned to a universal language that would eliminate misunderstanding and hatred in the world.
In 1901 he published "Hillelism" in Russian, in which he argued that the Zionist project would not solve the problems of the Jewish people.
He also published a religious philosophy called Homaranismo, based on the teachings of Hillel the Elder.
According to The Jewish Encyclopedia, he made several unsuccessful attempts to find a publisher.
For two years he tried to raise money for publication, until his future wife's father helped him with money.
In the end he found a publisher in Warsaw, Chaim Kelter.
The book first appeared in Russian on 26 July 1887.
Zamenhof signed it with the pen name Doktoro Esperanto.
According to the Ministry of Education booklet, he published the foundations of the language after ten years of work.
At the opening of the book he renounced all rights to the language and gave it to the public domain.
The name Esperanto for the language itself became established only in 1889, when people began using Zamenhof's pen name as the name of the language.
The publication of the book marks the beginning of the Esperanto movement.

stations.title: A second language for every person

paragraphs.text: According to The Jewish Encyclopedia, Zamenhof reached the conclusion that a language identified with a particular nationality or country would not become a universal medium of communication, and therefore it must be neutral.
Esperanto was meant to be a second language for every person in the world, alongside the mother tongue and not instead of it.
For him the language was also a way of promoting peaceful coexistence between different people and cultures.
In Esperanto nouns have no grammatical gender, so there is no need to wonder whether a table is masculine or feminine.
According to The Jewish Press, the language tried to combine ideas from Yiddish and from the structure of Hebrew.
According to the same newspaper, Zamenhof claimed that anyone could learn the language well in a week, and Tolstoy reportedly learned it in three to four hours.
At first, Zamenhof believed the project would appeal mainly to educated Jews like himself.
According to the Jewish Encyclopedia, in building the language he thought mainly of the needs of his own Yiddish-speaking people.
He described the Jews as locked up in a ghetto and exposed to the curse of ethnic hatred.
According to The Jewish Press, he wrote in 1905 that his Jewishness was the main reason he gave himself to the dream of the unity of humankind.

stations.title: From a pamphlet to a movement

paragraphs.text: According to The Jewish Encyclopedia, the success was immediate, and the language steadily gained popularity.
Before Esperanto there was the Volapük movement, and many of its members moved to the new language.
In 1897 Zamenhof settled in Warsaw, after moving from town to town, and worked long hours as an ophthalmologist.

According to The Jewish Press, the first congress, in 1905 in Boulogne-sur-Mer, brought together 700 participants from 20 countries, and more than 300 Esperanto associations were active around the world.
All the speeches were given in Esperanto, and people who could not otherwise communicate with each other conversed in it.
At the congress the movement was declared politically, religiously and morally neutral.
According to the Jewish Review of Books, in June 1906 some two hundred Jews were killed in a pogrom in Białystok, his native city.
In his speech at the congress in Geneva, Zamenhof said that the barriers between the nations were still appallingly high and thick, and that the Esperantists were laying siege to them.
He wrote a poem that was set to music, and to this day it is sung as an anthem at Esperanto gatherings.
In 1912, at the congress in Krakow, he stepped down from the leadership of the movement.
According to The Jewish Press, the First World War shattered Zamenhof's hopes, and together with his workload it harmed his health.
He died on 14 April 1917 in Warsaw.
He was buried in the Jewish cemetery on Okopowa Street.
Zamenhof's three children were murdered by the Nazis: Adam, the eldest, was shot near Warsaw, and Zofia was deported to Treblinka.
Lidia, who had joined the Bahá'í Faith, was murdered in Treblinka in September 1942.
Hitler saw Esperanto as evidence of a Jewish plot to take over the world.
The Gestapo received specific orders to search for Zamenhof's descendants.

stations.title: Recognition, and a language still spoken

paragraphs.text: The Universal Esperanto Association has been nominated for the Nobel Peace Prize more than a hundred times.
In 1954 the association became an official consultative organization of UNESCO.
UNESCO determined that what Esperanto had achieved in intellectual relations and in bringing peoples closer corresponds with its aims and its ideals.
In 1985 UNESCO encouraged countries to add Esperanto to their curricula.
Streets have been named after Zamenhof in many cities around the world, including Jerusalem and Tel Aviv.
The minor planet (1462) Zamenhof is also named after him.
Esperanto speakers celebrate his birthday, 15 December, every year as Zamenhof Day.
In the impression of the guide's author, in Białystok Zamenhof is the pride of the city.
The Zamenhof Center opened there on 15 December 2009, the 150th anniversary of his birth.
The Japanese religion Oomoto honors him as a deity and encourages its followers to use Esperanto.
Esperanto spread to Asia, America, the Middle East and Africa.
As of December 2020, 3.38 million learners had taken Duolingo's Esperanto courses.
The PAP agency reported that about thirty students complete an Esperanto course every day.
French intellectuals were more enthusiastic about Esperanto than the Jews of Russia, but they had a problem: it seemed too Jewish to them.
The Esperanto Committee went to great lengths to conceal Zamenhof's Jewishness, particularly from the French press.
According to the Jewish Review of Books, of 700 newspaper articles about the 1905 congress, only one mentioned that Zamenhof was Jewish.
At the world gathering in Krakow in 1912, Zamenhof himself blocked a request by a Jewish Esperantist to salute the gathering in the name of the Jewish people.
To criticism in a Yiddish newspaper in New York he replied that every Esperantist knows he is a Jew, because he never hid it.
In 1907 the movement split over reforms to the language, and the split gave rise to the planned language Ido.
An antisemitic weekly in Germany urged antisemites to learn Esperanto in order to communicate with antisemitic organizations in other countries.
In 1922 the French government banned the teaching of Esperanto at all French universities.
According to The Conversation, the Iranian delegate to the League of Nations proposed that Esperanto be adopted as the language of international relations.
According to a critique in The Jewish Press, in his drive to unite the world through Esperanto, Zamenhof rejected not only Zionism but also traditional Judaism.
According to the same newspaper, Esperanto remains largely a historical curiosity, and it must be viewed as a failure.

disagreements.question: How many roots does Esperanto have?

versions.says: The first book contains a dictionary with 917 roots
According to the Jewish Review of Books, the language was built on nine hundred roots from various European sources
According to the Ministry of Education booklet, the language has about 100 thousand roots
According to The Jewish Press, the language has about 900 roots common to many Romance languages

disagreements.question: How many times was Zamenhof nominated for the Nobel Peace Prize?

versions.says: According to The Jewish Press, 13 times, and he did not win
According to The Conversation, 14 nominations between 1907 and his death, and he did not win

disagreements.question: How many Esperanto speakers are there today?

versions.says: According to the Jewish Review of Books, by a generous estimate up to about two million people speak Esperanto, and perhaps about two thousand of them as a mother tongue.
According to The Jewish Press, about a million speakers and readers
According to the Ministry of Education booklet, about 1.5 million

disagreements.question: What did the League of Nations do with the proposal to adopt Esperanto?

versions.says: According to The Conversation, the French delegate vetoed it, fearing a decline in the standing of French in diplomacy
According to The Jewish Press, Esperanto's supporters failed to persuade the League of Nations to support it as an official international language

disagreements.question: How many Jews were killed in the Białystok pogrom of June 1906?

versions.says: According to the Jewish Review of Books: about two hundred
According to the Encyclopaedia Judaica (Jewish Virtual Library): 70 killed and 90 gravely injured
